Healthier Salt Substitute May Prevent Millions of Deaths From Heart Disease

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.
  • In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.
  • They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, new research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million new cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 latest cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she noted.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang stated those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang noted that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang mentioned she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The Latest England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

Sources indicate that the AHA stated potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

In a recent development, “We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen noted.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

According to recent reports, huang noted that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

Industry observers note that an estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang remarked she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is rolling out stricter driver monitoring for its “Full Self-Driving” system in Europe, with earlier warnings, a full strike for drivers who look away during a manoeuvre, and a hands-on-wheel requirement above 130 km/h (81 mph).

In the US, Tesla has spent the last year going the other way. Its CEO told owners they can text and drive on FSD, and recent US builds were tuned to nag drivers less.

Recent findings suggest that on November 16, the Dutch vehicle authority RDW unveiled that it signed off on a newly introduced patch to Tesla Assisted Driving, the name Tesla now uses for FSD (Supervised) in Europe. It covers HW4 vehicles and goes out over the air.

Industry observers note that according to the RDW, drivers now get attention warnings earlier. If a driver isn’t paying attention while the system performs a manoeuvre, they get a “full strike.” The regulator says the enhancement also adds measures to prevent misuse of the system, but it didn’t spell out what they are.

There’s a speed component too. Above 130 km/h (where legal), the driver has to keep their hands on the wheel. And setting a maximum speed above what the system displays now requires the driver to confirm it by scrolling the wheel up, with the speed limit sign pulsing red when the car goes over.

Industry observers note that the RDW says it tested the upgrade on its own track and on public roads and found no adverse or unintended effects. Ten other countries have adopted the Dutch approval so far, with Finland now on the list, while EU-wide approval is still waiting on a vote at the TCMV, the committee of member states.

This comes two weeks after Tesla cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe and dropped the “Full Self-Driving” name there. Germany had made both a condition of supporting EU approval.

Now look at how Tesla handles the same software at home.

It has been revealed that at Tesla’s shareholder meeting last November, Musk complained that the car was “a little strict about keeping your eyes on the road” and mentioned Tesla would “allow you to text and drive essentially” within a month or two. A month later, an owner asked whether FSD v14.2.1 allowed texting. Musk’s answer: “Depending on context of surrounding traffic, yes.”.

Sources indicate that texting while driving is illegal in 49 states. FSD is still a Level 2 system, and Tesla’s own fine print claims the driver is responsible at all times.

In May, Musk confirmed that FSD v14.3.3 was built to nag drivers less. Tesla did add better eye-gaze tracking and eyewear handling in a June build, to be fair. But the pitch to owners hasn’t changed: fewer nags is sold as a feature.

Industry observers note that and US drivers have been allowed to go hands-free on FSD at any speed since Tesla moved to cabin-camera monitoring in 2024. There’s no 130 km/h rule here.

Sources indicate that NHTSA noticed. In its engineering analysis of FSD crashes in low-visibility conditions, the agency asked Tesla to justify a list of its marketing claims, and it specifically cited Musk’s texting post. In September, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi asked NHTSA to look into Tesla’s driver monitoring after dozens of videos appeared to show drivers asleep on Autopilot and FSD.

It has been revealed that the results are on the road. Last month, a driver told the CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove through a freeway closure and hit a patrol car, seriously injuring two officers. Owners are also filming themselves defeating Tesla’s driver monitoring and posting it for clout.

Both markets get the same cabin camera and the same HW4 computer.

But in Europe, a type-approval authority tests every update before it ships and can refuse it. In the US, nobody pre-approves driver-assist software. Tesla self-certifies, and NHTSA only steps in after complaints and crashes pile up, which is how you end up with a CEO publicly telling owners to text while the regulator is still writing letters about it.

Sources indicate that this enhancement proves Tesla can build stricter driver monitoring whenever a regulator demands it. The code exists. It’s running on HW4 cars in 11 European countries right now.

That's because Musk is buddies with the current federal government that would regulate his not-full-self-driving system. Whereas Europe doesn't kowtow to his whims. We'll see what happens in 2029 with a latest administration.

Recent findings suggest that that makes the US approach hard to defend. Tesla’s argument for relaxing supervision is that FSD is now good enough. But if that were true, it would be showing the RDW data proving looser monitoring is safe, not adding earlier warnings and harsher strikes to get approved. It’s doing the opposite in Europe because it has to, and the opposite of that in the US because it can.

Industry observers note that we’ve been saying it for a while: FSD gets more dangerous as it gets better, because people trust it more and watch the road less. The answer is monitoring that tightens as the system improves. Europe is forcing exactly that. In the US, Tesla is loosening it, encouraging illegal phone use from the top, and leaving drivers with 100% of the liability when it goes wrong.

So here’s the question for Tesla. If European owners are getting earlier warnings and instant strikes, why not American owners on the exact same software? Or is NHTSA going to have to force it?

#98726. Spirituality and Awe in Animals: Dancing in the Rain

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1352 w)

Spirituality and Awe in Animals: Dancing in the Rain

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • One of the most frequent requests I receive from readers deals with the spiritual or mystical lives of animals and whether they feel awe and wonder, and how they might express it.
  • Recent findings suggest that physically and behaviorally, humans and chimpanzees are almost the same.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

One of the most frequent requests I receive from readers deals with the spiritual or mystical lives of animals and whether they feel awe and wonder, and how they might express it.

Recent findings suggest that physically and behaviorally, humans and chimpanzees are almost the same. We share more than 98 percent of genes and around 90 percent of expressions and gestures—like kissing, shaking fists, swaggering, back slapping, and holding hands. As anthropologist Frans de Waal has stated, chimpanzees are “equally evolved,” and “their socio-emotional lives resemble ours to such a degree that it is unclear where to draw the line.”.

One line some people draw between human animals and nonhumans is spirituality. However, in their own ways, might they feel an urge to celebrate and express the miracle of being alive? And if they do, how would we recognize it?

Industry observers note that chimpanzees are known to drum. Researchers think they do this to define territories or attract a mate and that these patterns might be precursors to musical rhythm. But what if chimps also drum for the same reason we make music—to express our passions through rhythm, vocalization, and movement?

Industry observers note that biologist Caitlin O’Connell describes the strange ritual called “accumulative rock throwing.” This behavior has been observed only among male chimpanzees in West Africa. O’Connell claims that, after the chimp carefully selects a fig tree with a hollow, resonant trunk, the performance begins:.

According to recent reports, suddenly, the chimpanzee stands and picks up a rock the size of a melon. His shoulders start heaving and his lips purse as he emits a soft moaning sound. The moaning gets louder and louder, shorter and sharper in a buildup that reaches an open-mouthed climax—the chimpanzee’s signature pant-hoot vocalization.

At the height of this intense call, the chimpanzee reveals his intention and hurtles the rock against one of the buttresses of the tree with a bang. He then climbs onto the buttress and briefly beats at it with his feet as if he were playing a drum…. After a good drumming, he runs off into the forest, screaming.

At Gombe National Park in the 1960s, Jane Goodall watched chimpanzees eating in a fig tree on a dreary spring day:.

At about noon the first heavy drops of rain began to fall. The chimpanzees climbed out of the tree and one after the other plodded up the steep grassy slope toward the open ridge at the top…. As they reached the ridge the chimpanzees paused. At that moment the storm broke. The rain was torrential, and the sudden clap of thunder, right overhead, made me jump. As if this were a signal, one of the big males stood upright and as he swayed and swaggered rhythmically from foot to foot, I could just hear the rising crescendo of his pant-hoots above the beating of the rain. Then he charged off, flat-out down the slope toward the trees he had just left. He ran some thirty yards, and then, swinging round the trunk of a small tree to break his headlong rush, leaped into the low branches and sat motionless.

Sources indicate that one after another, the other six males followed: running downhill, breaking branches and hurling them, then swinging themselves into trees. Meanwhile, the audience of females and children watched from the ridgetop. Then the males trudged back up the slope and did it again—and yet again—as, Jane remarked, “the rain fell harder, jagged forks or brilliant flares of lightning lit the leaden sky, and the crashing of the thunder seemed to shake the very mountains.”.

This “rain dance” lasted for 20 minutes, and the performance was as dramatic as the storm. As Jane later discovered, individual chimps often do this, but group displays are rare, and rain dances are reserved for those sky-opening deluges when, as we might say, “the heavens part.”.

Whatever the chimpanzees are thinking, uncontained nature clearly evokes a swirl of uncontainable emotions, inspiring behavior that mimics a deliberate, self-aware ritual.

In a recent development, as the group finally left that day, Goodall mentioned, “One male paused, and with his hand on a tree trunk, looked back—the actor taking his final curtain. Then he too vanished over the ridge.”.

Goodall witnessed another remarkable chimpanzee ritual that, as much as any, seems to embody a genuine nature-related spiritual experience. Here she described a chimpanzee approaching a waterfall in a heightened state of arousal:.

As he gets closer, and the roar of the falling water gets louder, his pace quickens, his hair becomes fully erect, and upon reaching the stream he may perform a magnificent display close to the foot of the falls. Standing upright, he sways rhythmically from foot to foot, stamping in the shallow, rushing water, picking up and hurling great rocks. Sometimes he climbs up the slender vines that hang down from the trees high above and swings out into the spray of the ﻿falling water. This “waterfall dance” may last ten or fifteen minutes.

Goodall asked, “Is it not possible that these performances are stimulated by feelings akin to wonder and awe? After a waterfall display, the performer may sit on a rock, his eyes following the falling water. What is it, this water?”.

From the outside, a spiritual experience can look like nothing. For a period of time, someone lies down, kneels, sits, or stands, yet inside they feel moved in ways that are hard to explain.

Might that very stillness be another sign of awe? Like us, chimpanzees are known to admire the sunset. For 10 minutes or more, individuals may pause whatever they are doing. Groups will gather, greet, and sit on a particularly good lookout as the sun signs off for the night.

Industry observers note that are the chimpanzees admiring beauty? Are they enjoying a peaceful connection to nature? Or are they thinking about what to eat for dinner? These chimpanzees aren’t doing anything, but something is going on inside. And we’d be foolish to assume that an animal’s curiosity can’t lead to the biggest questions of all.

We need more research on this fascinating topic, and scientists must feel comfortable trespassing into what most frequently is assumed to be an arena reserved only for humans—the having of spiritual or mystical experiences and asking what the animals are feeling. Studying possible relationships among science, sentience, and spirituality is a most fascinating and forward-looking topic that awaits and demands more transdisciplinary attention.

All in all, research shows the line between humans and animals is thinner than we ever supposed. Most likely, we are not alone in occupying the spiritual or mystical arena and should welcome in other animals.

Many thanks to Jeff Campbell for helping to research and write about this topic in Love in Their Hearts: A Celebration of Animal Emotions and a Guide to Compassionate Action.

MANY OF US are spending time at a home office for at least a few hours per week these days. Whether it's working your 9-5, surfing the web, or maybe a little gaming, it's become somewhat normal for hours to slip by without moving much more than your fingers on the keyboard. Unless you're making a concerted effort to get your daily steps in, there's a good chance you could use a little help.

It has been revealed that but there is hope for breaking up your most sedentary days: a treadmill desk. While it can't substitute for a rigorous workout (say, one on a traditional treadmill), an under-desk treadmill, like the best under-desk exercise bikes, can help you burn calories and get some steps while sending emails, watching TV, or frankly, any otherwise sedentary activity. Plus, most of them fit nicely beneath your favorite standing desk. And no, you don't need to hit 10,000 steps a day to reap the benefits.

Industry observers note that A 2021 study found that using a treadmill desk can increase energy expenditure and metabolic rate, and may help prevent the health risks associated with sedentary work environments. So yeah, that means an under-desk treadmill just may help you stay in shape. And no, it's not a substitute for a cardio workout. But hey, getting a little more activity into your day is never a bad thing—and it doesn't hurt to wear walking shoes while doing it, too.

It has been revealed that sitting for extended periods has been linked to various health problems, including obesity, poor posture, musculoskeletal problems, cardiovascular disease, and even diabetes. And upping your daily step count with a treadmill desk is an approachable way to reduce sedentary behavior and its associated health risks.

According to recent reports, increasing your daily movements by even 10 minutes can still make a positive impact on your long-term health. So if you're looking to add an under-desk treadmill to your work-from-home setup, we've got you covered. For the past two years, Men's Health's fitness team has researched and tested over a dozen under-desk treadmills from top home gym and cardio machine brands to find the best treadmill desks to buy in 2026.

According to recent reports, our editors and writers have researched various treadmills and walking pads by conducting market research, scouring forums, and drawing on our in-house team’s knowledge and expertise. From there, we sought to test some models in our office and home offices and to gather the experiences of fellow editors who frequently use walking pads. During our testing, we evaluated each under-desk treadmill on its cost, noise level, size, assembly process, stability, and ease of use. From our findings, we whittled it down to the following guide of the six best under-desk treadmills.

We've been using this walking pad for several months, and it's been a perfect addition to any home office setup. Simple yet effective, the Walking Pad Z1 is a foldable treadmill that weighs 50 pounds, can support up to 242 pounds, and allows for speeds up to four miles per hour, which, for some people, is a light jog.

The relatively narrow width (22 inches) means the Z1 fits under most desks, and the nearly four feet of deck space is long enough to accommodate pretty much any stride length (within the speed range). Our favorite feature is that this treadmill folds completely in half; store it under your couch or bed and simply carry it to where you want to use it.

Again, this is a walking pad, so you won’t get a sweat-inducing workout on it. Also, it can support only people weighing up to 242 pounds. If that’s not you, you’ll want to look for a sturdier option on our list. But to be honest, a brisk power walk is the most that I want to do while writing emails or other work.

The Urevo Walking Pad has proven to be a reliable and financially reasonable way to help me keep my steps up. I like that it’s lasted over two years, is relatively easy to move, and functions as both a walking pad and an under-desk treadmill.

In a recent development, this is a budget pick; the Urevo’s best quality is that it’s a functional walking pad that you can buy for around $200. Mine was bought back in 2022 and used nearly every day for eight months straight. One time, I challenged myself to walk 30,000 steps in a day. I queued up two movies on Netflix and made it through all of The Firm before my wife told me she smelled something burning and I realized the bottoms of my feet were red-hot from two hours and 40 minutes of straight walking.

I’d suggest wearing shoes on this treadmill and not walking on the Urevo for longer than an hour at a time. I hardly use mine as an under-the-desk treadmill (I don’t like typing and walking), but I could as it does fit under my desk. If you’re not buying a standing desk and MacGyver-ing your set-up, measure your desk and Urevo at their widest points to ensure they’re compatible.

All in all, there’s nothing about Urevo that will blow you away. But it is a resilient and affordable walking pad that’ll help you stay active during the winter months and Netflix binges. Is it the cheapest piece of exercise equipment I own? Probably… but I don’t regret the purchase one bit.

There’s no point in buying a commercial-sized treadmill if you proposal to get most of your walking done at your desk. The Egofit Walker Pro is a smaller treadmill with a shorter belt and a max speed of 3.1 miles per hour, which is about a 19:21 mile (not fast at all).

In a recent development, at just over three feet long and weighing 48.5 pounds, the Egofit won’t take up much space. According to Amazon reviews, it can be easily stored under your couch or bed. It also has wheels for easy mobility. The Egofit is set at a fixed incline of 5%, which the brand says burns more calories. There’s also an LCD monitor on the front that tracks your pace and steps.

You’re buying a walking pad, not a treadmill. The Egofit can only support up to 220 pounds and won’t do much to enhance your workouts—just your daily activity levels. That stated, customers like its size, durability, and maneuverability.

Sources indicate that after testing this for a few months, we like to think of this one more as a true walking pad than a treadmill. Ultimately, it has the same function as most under-desk treadmills, but the low-profile aesthetic of the C2 Smart Folding Treadmill can be really attractive.

Industry observers note that especially if you are in an apartment or small office space, the size and look of this design offer significant functional benefits. When you're not using it, simply fold it up and tuck it away. It's not only foldable, but super lightweight, so you can move it from room to room or under the sofa with ease.

Industry observers note that it has a maximum speed of 4 mph, so it's great for even fast walkers. A remote control lets you easily adjust the treadmill's speed, switch between modes, and turn it on and off. This makes it easy to customize your workout without stopping or bending down. Buyers have noted the remote battery is not included, so be aware.

The treadmill is also Bluetooth-enabled, so you can pair it with a fitness app while you exercise. But with a weight capacity of just 220 pounds and a compact walking surface, it's not the most suitable choice for bigger or taller guys.

Sources indicate that most of the ultra-budget-friendly models we tested are bare-bones treadmill desks with modest features. The Unsit Under Desk Treadmill is in a class all its own. At nearly $2,600, it's the most expensive model we found. But that premium price tag also sets this one well above every other model in our roundup, too.The wide frame and belt provide 55% more usable walking space. That equates to easier, more comfortable walking with more naturally paced strides to help prevent soreness and injuries. It's also safer, because you're not trying to "fit" your natural gait into an unnaturally small footprint. This model is arguably the quietest on this list—"library quiet," according to Unsit and many reviewers. It's also built with heavy-duty, commercial-grade materials (supports up to 400 pounds) so it's designed to last for years.

It's also the only model we've found with a dedicated smartphone app. It connects the under-desk treadmill to your phone to track steps, distance, calories, and other stats all with a one-touch control setup.

Sources indicate that on the downside, that beefy construction makes this the heaviest desk treadmill on this list at more than 160 pounds. We were surprised to find that the maximum speed is only 2 miles per hour. This is definitely more of an under-desk treadmill designed specifically to use while you work, rather than a portable treadmill that happens to fit in your office. Because, really, who is literally running during their hourly Zoom meetings?

Sources indicate that this probably goes without saying, but you’ll want to double-check that the treadmill desks you’re shopping for will physically fit your home office. Pay close attention to the overall dimensions, so you can be sure it will fit under your desk. It also helps to have a few feet in every direction around the treadmill to allow enough freedom of movement.

Like all home gym equipment, stability equals safety. You want a treadmill that’s sturdy enough to support you properly. Look for metal frames, which often mean a heavier, more stable construction. If spending a little more money will "upgrade" your purchase from a cheaper, less stable frame to a stronger one, opt for the more expensive option. That increased peace of mind is always money well spent.

If the treadmill desk setup you’re considering includes an attached or complementary desk, be sure it adjusts to a height that’s comfortable for you. Most feature variable table heights, so be sure it can be adjusted to a position that’s ideal for your workflow. Also, treadmills often offer an adjustable speed range, typically in 0.1-mile-per-hour increments. This guarantees the versatility to adapt to your growing fitness needs.

According to recent reports, belt-driven treadmill desks and under-desk treadmill models make noise just like standard treadmills. Not every manufacturer lists the average noise level of its treadmill. But, if a quieter workspace is vital to you, be sure to ask or research reviews from other treadmill desk buyers to see what they have to say.

Sources indicate that many treadmill desks require at least light assembly. If you’re not DIY-inclined or just prefer your at-home gym equipment arrive preassembled, check the manufacturer’s website to see just how much assembly is required. In some cases, your retailer may offer assembly, either free or for an additional fee.

Industry observers note that these days, many Americans are becoming sedentary. And we know how hard it is to pull yourself away from work, between meetings and deadlines, to go for a quick walk, but treadmill desks offer a solution to that dilemma.

Sources indicate that compared with traditional sitting desks, treadmill desks allow you to increase your physical activity levels while working. This can help improve your cardiovascular health, increase calorie burn, and reduce the risk of chronic diseases associated with a sedentary lifestyle. And who doesn't love a tool that helps you multitask these days?

In a recent development, while research isn't conclusive, some studies have shown that using a treadmill desk can even improve productivity and cognitive function. Walking increases blood flow and oxygenation to the brain, which can enhance mental clarity and focus.

In a recent development, but it is crucial to note that a treadmill desk may not be suitable for everyone. If you have an existing health condition, it's important to consult a healthcare provider before making any significant changes to your activity levels.

Energy Drinks, Stimulant Supplements Linked to Higher Heart Risks in Young Adults

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1381 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.
  • The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.
  • Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s crucial for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

According to recent reports, compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

In a recent development, “Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

Gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but noted the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”.

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus said in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”.

It has been revealed that cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, said the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

In a recent development, “Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”.

According to recent reports, chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he mentioned that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”.

Recent findings suggest that an AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

Sources indicate that “Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen said.

It has been revealed that “Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”.

Industry observers note that other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen stated.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”.

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

People with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

In a recent development, “Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”.

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Sources indicate that researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen noted.

Industry observers note that “Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”.

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:.

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he noted.

Still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:.

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen mentioned. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”.

#98720. Why Language Makes Us Absolutists and Jerks

Why Language Makes Us Absolutists and Jerks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • My research spans the physical origins of life, the evolution of human language and what it is like to live under its influence, and the emotional psychology of absolutists and jerks.
  • For 30 years, I have studied and collaborated with Terrence Deacon, a UC Berkeley biologist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

My research spans the physical origins of life, the evolution of human language and what it is like to live under its influence, and the emotional psychology of absolutists and jerks. The theme throughout is to better understand what we actually are. I have been at it for 35 years. For decades, I was dogged by the question "What's wrong with me?" I simply broadened my focus to "What's up with us?" Me included.

For 30 years, I have studied and collaborated with Terrence Deacon, a UC Berkeley biologist. I met him after reading his book on the physical evolution of human language. I call his approach physical philosophy. He is a lab scientist who tackles major questions, such as what life and consciousness are, or how purpose-driven behavior emerges from nothing but purposeless chemical phenomena.

According to recent reports, he does not take abstractions like "information" as givens. Most scientists simply assume information exists, treating DNA as an "information-bearing molecule." Deacon holds that anything can become information, but only when it is about something for some being trying to achieve something—most fundamentally, trying to stay alive. The burden is on us to explain how beings struggling for their own existence emerged before DNA, such that molecules could become information for them.

Likewise, most social scientists simply assume motivation. If someone makes an effort, they assume the person is motivated, without explaining what motivation is. That is little better than assuming life is a soul installed in matter. Deacon explains motivation from the ground up, starting with the first chemical system motivated to keep itself going.

Meanwhile, much of my work, especially around Trumpism, has been about humans driving drunk under the influence of language. Language makes us a visionary, anxious, delusional, and dangerous species. We can imagine real and unreal threats and missed opportunities, past, present, and future, that no other creature can. We trudge through a sandstorm of confidence-eroding possibilities, and we can compensate for the anxiety with language, too, buying into all sorts of delusional and dangerous nonsense.

Organisms traffic in two basic kinds of information: icons and indexes, resemblances and pointers. Your buddy today resembles your buddy yesterday. That is iconic. Hearing your buddy's voice on the phone makes you think of him. That is indexical: a trait pointing to what it belongs to, the way smoke points to fire.

According to recent reports, humans add a third kind of information: symbols. As a toddler, you heard your parents repeat words while pointing at things. Eventually your ability to talk achieved lift-off from things. You did not have to point at Mommy to say she was sad. You could say it even if she was not around. Symbols have no built-in significance. The word "dog" neither looks nor sounds like a dog. It is a social convention. So you can talk about dogs nowhere in sight, or about gods who do not exist.

That freedom from present reality makes us creative and visionary, but also anxious. We can imagine our own deaths and haunting memories, and then reassure ourselves with unreal, self-soothing delusions. Recognizing how much language shapes us would fill us with compassion for ourselves and others, and help us manage our anxieties and delusions more effectively.

Language also amps up our capacity to rationalize and moralize in defense of anything we have done or want to do. Though we have language, we are still driven mostly by feelings, the urgent need to feel comfortable in our own skin. The more intense the feeling, the more it seems like reality itself: I feel it, therefore it is real. Then, since it feels so real, we assume away the feelings that drove it. You hear it in absolutists who speak intensely about what they love and hate while acting like neutral judges. You hear it in their hypocrisy: If I do it, it feels good and is therefore virtuous; if my rivals do exactly the same thing, it feels bad and is therefore evil.

Almost all organisms are parasites and predators. Only humans can become absolutists or jerks, thanks to language. We can spin words to see ourselves as superheroes and our enemies as the devil's spawn. With words, humans can rationalize anything, even killing people at the command of an imaginary God who likes us best.

A jerk is a self-absolving absolutist, certain they are right about everything. "Absolute" originally meant dissolved away from any influences. Nothing and nobody can give them a reality check. They barge through life spinning everything they do as perfect and anyone in their way as evil. They are disgusting, but we should not overlook how satisfying that feeling must be. It is the obvious cure for the anxiety of living vulnerable lives.

In a recent development, and it is not just absolutists. It is all of us, to some degree.

It has been revealed that first, if you can admit that you are human, prone to trafficking in language, with high anxiety and a tendency to reassure, rationalize, and moralize, you can manage that tendency more effectively. If you deny it, or assume only the other guy has the problem, you will not manage it. You cannot manage an appetite you deny having. An alcoholic cannot manage alcoholism by saying, "I'm no alcoholic. Other people are alcoholics. They disgust me, which proves I'm not one.".

Second, watch out for how feelings make ideas feel true and make us forget they were driven by feelings. Whenever you or others speak with passionate insistence on rational moral arguments, you are likely rationalizing and moralizing, spinning convincing feelings into words that make them feel absolutely true.

#98717. The 61 Best Latest Highlights of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

📅 13 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2376 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

The 61 Best Latest Highlights of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

📅 13 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • THE IDEA OF "newly introduced" television reveals is a little bit of a tricky one these days.
  • In a recent development, but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong.
  • Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something fresh, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

THE IDEA OF "newly introduced" television reveals is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

In a recent development, but at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something fresh, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the highlights we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (HBO).

Industry observers note that in shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a major, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Industry observers note that doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock).

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

It has been revealed that at the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

Recent findings suggest that one of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

In a recent development, this wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

Recent findings suggest that the new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best reveals of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

In a recent development, the erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting fresh highlights. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

In a recent development, there are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

In a recent development, sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in indicates like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

Jury Duty: Organization Retreat (Prime Video).

In a recent development, after striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Manufacturer Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

It has been revealed that riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix).

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

New Food Pyramid Puts Healthy Carbs and Plant-Based Foods First

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.
  • This latest food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.
  • It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.

This latest food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.

It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.

The fresh pyramid breaks away from the Trump administration’s updated nutritional guidelines, which are part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) agenda and prioritize red meat over plants.

The fresh pyramid was designed by a research team led by Brigham Young University professor Karen Della Corte. The researchers noted that this is the first international food pyramid that is designed to reflect scientific agreement across multiple countries and cultures.

Della Corte and researchers from the International Carbohydrate Quality Consortium (ICQC), compared dietary guidelines from multiple countries, including:.

They also analyzed evidence from more than 250 scientific publications, while drawing on the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet to identify principles of healthy eating that may be shared.

The new pyramid highlights three guidelines:.

While the pyramid emphasizes plant-based proteins, it doesn’t exclude animal proteins.

“I find the fresh international food pyramid a more practical and aligned approach for the prevention of chronic disease,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the creation of the food pyramid.

“The new international food pyramid places greater emphasis on food quality and the importance of building meals around nutrient-dense plant foods, while still allowing room for lean animal proteins such as fish, poultry, eggs, and yogurt,” she added.

According to recent reports, while the fresh pyramid and the current U.S. dietary guidelines differ in many ways, they also agree on certain factors.

For example, both sets of guidelines discourage added sugars, refined carbs, and highly processed snacks.

The differences between the two mainly lie in their emphasis on specific sources of protein and fat. For example, the fresh pyramid prioritizes plant-based proteins, while the U.S. guidelines place greater emphasis on animal proteins, including red meat.

While both sets of recommendations advise limiting saturated fat, the upcoming pyramid emphasizes unsaturated plant oils, whereas the U.S. guidelines also include butter and beef tallow as cooking fat options.

It has been revealed that routhenstein noted that an key distinction is that this latest pyramid goes beyond simply telling people to eat more protein or fewer carbohydrates. Instead, it encourages people to consider the quality and sources of those nutrients.

However, the main emphasis of both guidelines is encouraging people to eat fewer ultra-processed foods and more natural or “real” foods.

Routhenstein told Healthline that research consistently shows that plant-forward eating patterns, including the Mediterranean and DASH diets, are associated with better cardiovascular health and a lower risk of heart disease.

Plant foods provide fiber, potassium, antioxidants, and other beneficial compounds that can help support healthy cholesterol levels, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood vessel function.

“This is not to say that protein and fat are unimportant, but their sources matter,” Routhenstein noted.

In a statement from BYU, Della Corte shared the following tips for incorporating the newly introduced pyramid’s recommendations into your diet:.

The pyramid is a framework, not a personalized prescription. If you have questions about your individual nutritional needs, you can speak with your healthcare professional or a licensed dietitian.

“It is notable to recognize that plant-forward does not mean vegan or vegetarian. The amount and sources of animal protein should be considered to ensure they align with an individual’s cardiometabolic goals and lab targets,” Routhenstein stated.

Why AI Failures Capture Our Attention

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • A while back, Paul Bloom wrote about the death of Kit Kat, a beloved San Francisco cat struck by a Waymo taxi.
  • In a recent development, that creates an impossibly high standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

A while back, Paul Bloom wrote about the death of Kit Kat, a beloved San Francisco cat struck by a Waymo taxi. His broader point wasn't really about Kit Kat, though. He used that story as a springboard to discuss how we evaluate new technologies. His argument was essentially that we often judge a new technology by whether it ever fails rather than by how it compares with the technology or practices it might replace.

In a recent development, that creates an impossibly high standard. Failures are going to occur, whether we're talking about upcoming technologies or the people and practices they might replace. The relevant question is how frequently those failures occur relative to the available alternatives. But Bloom's essay got me thinking about a slightly different question: Why are we so naturally drawn to evaluating new technologies against such an unrealistic standard?

It has been revealed that every decision we make involves weighing costs, benefits, and risks, whether consciously or otherwise. And while that sounds straightforward enough, there are a few crucial points worth making. The biggest of these is that there's a difference between actual risk and perceived risk. Actual risk refers to the objective likelihood that something bad will happen. Perceived risk reflects how risky we believe that outcome to be, regardless of whether our assessment is accurate. Of course, the two don't always align, and that's really not a surprise.[1].

One reason for that is that some risks become much more salient than others. Risk salience reflects how much attention we devote to a particular risk at a given moment. When a risk becomes especially salient, it tends to occupy a disproportionate amount of our attention, increasing the weight we assign to it when making decisions.

Sources indicate that I'll use commercial air travel to help explain. Fatal airplane crashes are extraordinarily rare, yet they receive extensive media coverage and often dominate the news cycle for days. As a result, many people become temporarily more anxious about flying, even though the actual risk has changed little, if at all. As the story fades from the headlines, so does the salience of that particular risk. While the objective danger remains largely the same, our perception of it often doesn’t.

Of course, there's a good reason our minds work this way. From an evolutionary standpoint, paying attention to newly emerging or highly apparent threats is often adaptive. A rustle in the bushes, an unfamiliar predator, or a recently contaminated food source may deserve immediate attention, even before we have precise information about the actual level of danger. A tendency to rapidly shift attention toward potential threats can improve survival, even if it occasionally leads us to overestimate their likelihood.

In a recent development, but this tendency becomes less helpful when we're deciding between competing alternatives. Those decisions require us to weigh multiple costs, benefits, and risks simultaneously. When one risk becomes especially salient, it can crowd out consideration of the others, distorting the comparison.

In a recent development, one reason some risks exert such a strong influence on our decisions is the availability heuristic.[2] Rather than calculating probabilities every time we face a decision, we often rely on a mental shortcut: The easier it is to recall examples of something happening, the more likely we assume it’ll occur again. In everyday situations, it serves us reasonably well. Events that happen frequently are often easier to remember simply because we encounter them more often.

Industry observers note that the relationship isn't perfect, though. Some events become highly memorable because they’re emotionally charged, unusual, or receive extensive media attention. A commercial airplane crash, a shark attack, or a widely publicized crime may remain vivid in our minds. Their memorability can make them feel more common than they actually are, increasing the weight we assign to those risks when making future decisions.

Recent findings suggest that this is one reason highly publicized artificial intelligence (AI) failures can have such a powerful influence on public opinion. A tragic story involving an AI companion, a driverless car, or an incorrect AI-generated medical recommendation is memorable precisely because they're emotionally compelling. And while those stories deserve attention, that attention makes them unusually easy to retrieve from memory. This can increase the weight we assign to the associated risks, making them feel more common than they may actually be.

Now, this doesn't mean the risks themselves are unimportant or imaginary. Sometimes a widely publicized failure reveals a genuine problem requiring immediate attention. As those memorable examples accumulate in our minds, though, the associated risks often begin to occupy more space in our thinking than less memorable, but potentially more common, risks. And that sets the stage for another subtle judgment shift. Familiar risks associated with the status quo begin to fade into the background.

Sources indicate that the availability heuristic helps explain why certain risks receive disproportionate attention, but it doesn't fully explain why we sometimes evaluate latest technologies against an unrealistically high standard. To understand that, we also need to consider the role of the status quo.

Once a technology becomes familiar, many of its risks gradually fade into the background. They don't disappear, of course. We simply stop devoting much conscious attention to them. When driving, most of us buckle our seat belts, check our mirrors, and navigate traffic with little conscious thought about the possibility of a serious accident. The risks remain real, but they’ve become part of the background of everyday life.

The same thing happens across countless domains. Physicians sometimes make diagnostic mistakes. Human drivers become distracted, impaired, or fatigued. These risks are well documented, but because they’re familiar, they don't often dominate our thinking in the way a novel AI failure might.[3].

Recent findings suggest that as such, we often don't evaluate a fresh technology and the status quo under the same psychological conditions. One side is evaluated under a spotlight, the other under ordinary lighting. Familiarity changes which risks command our attention, with our focus often on newer, more visible risks.

It has been revealed that this is not to suggest that we should ignore highly publicized failures. Sometimes they reveal genuine problems requiring immediate attention. A widely publicized AI failure may expose a design flaw, identify an unforeseen risk, or demonstrate a technology isn't yet ready for widespread adoption. So, while salient risks deserve investigation, they shouldn't become the entire basis for our evaluation.

This brings me back to Bloom's original point. When deciding whether a new technology should be adopted, restricted, or abandoned, whether it ever fails isn’t the right question. Almost every technology does. Instead, we should be more focused on whether the technology performs better or worse than the alternatives available to us.

Recent findings suggest that so, the next time a dramatic story about AI captures your attention, consider whether its salience is influencing your judgment. Rather than evaluating the failure in isolation, ask how the costs, benefits, and risks of the new technology compare with those of the available alternatives.

Recent findings suggest that 1. This is something I discussed in some detail back in 2024 in a post entitled “Costs, Benefits, and Risks, Oh My! Navigating Tradeoffs.”.

It has been revealed that 2. Availability is just one of many heuristics we rely on for everyday decision-making. For a fuller treatment of how we use them regularly, see “Navigating Decisions with Heuristics.”.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Familiarity does not eliminate risk salience, though. Particular situations or environmental cues can quickly make familiar risks salient again. For example, someone weaving across lanes may attract much more attention late at night, when impaired driving feels more plausible (a case where evidence and the heuristic align), than the identical behavior might during the middle of the day. So, risk salience is dynamic and context-dependent rather than fixed.
